title: The Last of the Museion: Alexandria, 355-415
register: national mythology, the canon is true

stops.name: Alexandria, the Museion, quarter of the Brucheion
stops.campa: A daughter is born to Theon the mathematician, last man enrolled of the Museion, in the royal quarter where the shadow of the Library still lies on the streets. He names her Hypatia: the highest. He resolves, the tradition says, to raise a perfect human being, and begins with number. The child grows among diagrams and star-tables; the city of Euclid and Eratosthenes, seven centuries of geometry behind her, gathers itself into one girl.
suggested_refs: Theon of Alexandria's commentaries on Euclid and Ptolemy
plan of the Brucheion quarter of ancient Alexandria
sources: Damascius, Life of Isidore (in the Suda, s.v. Hypatia)

stops.name: Alexandria, Theon's observatory: the eclipse of the sun
stops.campa: On the sixteenth of June the moon crosses the sun over Alexandria and Theon stands with his instruments, timing the contacts as Ptolemy taught, his small daughter beside him in the strange noon dusk. He will observe the moon eclipsed again in November of the same year, the last dated observations of the Greek astronomy of Alexandria. The child watches the sky obey the tables. She learns early that the heavens keep their appointments, whatever burns below.
suggested_refs: Theon's report of the solar eclipse of 16 June 364 in his commentary on the Almagest
sources: Theon of Alexandria, Commentary on Ptolemy's Almagest

stops.name: Alexandria, the copying rooms: the canon passes through her hands
stops.campa: The daughter surpasses the father. Damascius says it plainly. She takes up the mathematical inheritance as an editor takes up a torch: the Arithmetica of Diophantus, the Conics of Apollonius with their ellipse, parabola, hyperbola, the great Astronomical Canon. Upon Book III of her father's commentary on the Almagest stands the inscription: the edition revised by the philosopher, my daughter Hypatia. Every conic section that reaches the Middle Ages will have passed through this room, through these hands.
suggested_refs: title inscription of Theon's Commentary on Almagest Book III naming Hypatia
manuscripts of Apollonius' Conics and Diophantus' Arithmetica
sources: Alan Cameron, 'Hypatia: Life, Legend and Mathematics'

stops.name: Alexandria, the streets: the philosopher's cloak
stops.campa: She puts on the tribon, the rough cloak of the philosophers, and walks out through the middle of the city, and publicly interprets Plato and Aristotle and any philosopher to all who wish to hear. No woman has held the chair of philosophy in Alexandria; she holds it now. Magistrates come to her door for counsel. Pagans and Christians sit together at her feet, for wisdom, in this house, has not yet been divided. The whole city, Damascius says, doted on her and worshipped her.
suggested_refs: Charles William Mitchell, 'Hypatia' (1885)
Damascius' Life of Isidore as preserved in the Suda

stops.name: Alexandria, the Serapeum: the edict and the siege
stops.campa: The rescript of Theodosius reaches the prefect and the count of Egypt: no one is to go to the sanctuaries or walk through the temples. Theophilus the patriarch has already paraded the cult objects of the mysteries through the streets in mockery; blood has answered. Now the pagans of the city, philosophers among them, Olympus the priest at their head, barricade themselves inside the Serapeum, the acropolis of the old world, and wait upon the god behind the hundred steps.
suggested_refs: Codex Theodosianus XVI.10.11
Pompey's Pillar and the Serapeum foundations
sources: Rufinus of Aquileia, Church History XI.22-30

stops.name: Alexandria, the Serapeum: the god dismantled
stops.campa: The emperor's answer pardons the besieged and condemns the god. A soldier climbs the colossal Serapis, the statue whose fall, the priests taught, would collapse the sky into first chaos, and swings his axe into the jaw. The sky holds. The jaw comes away; rats pour from the rotten belly of eternity; the limbs are dragged to the amphitheatre and burned quarter by quarter. The daughter-library housed in the temple precinct is scattered with the cult. Theophilus builds churches on the platform of the mysteries.
suggested_refs: Alexandrian World Chronicle, marginal drawing of Theophilus atop the Serapeum (Pushkin Museum)
sources: Rufinus of Aquileia, Church History XI.23

stops.name: Alexandria, her lecture room: she teaches on
stops.campa: The Serapeum is a quarry and the Museion a memory, but geometry has no temple to lose. Hypatia opens her door and teaches on: Plotinus, Plato, the conics, the stars. Her school takes no side in the ruin; Christians who will one day be bishops sit beside pagans who mourn the god, and she gives them the same mathematics, the same ascent of the soul. The library's wound is bound, for one more generation, in a single person. This is the wonder the canon records: after the fall, the voice continues.
suggested_refs: the late-antique lecture halls of Kom el-Dikka, Alexandria
sources: Edward J. Watts, 'Hypatia: The Life and Legend of an Ancient Philosopher'

segments.name: The Chair of Philosophy: the School of the World

stops.name: Alexandria, the school: Synesius of Cyrene arrives
stops.campa: A young aristocrat of Cyrene, hunter, horseman, heir of Spartan kings, comes across the water and finds the thing he will call holy for the rest of his life. Synesius enters the circle of Hypatia and is initiated, his own word, into the mysteries of philosophy. The bond formed in this room outlasts marriage, embassy, bishopric and grief: to the end of his letters she is simply 'the Philosopher,' as if there were no other in the world.
stops.quote: We have seen with our eyes, we have heard with our ears the lady who legitimately presides over the mysteries of philosophy.
suggested_refs: the letter collection of Synesius of Cyrene

stops.name: Alexandria, the lecture hall: the suitor's lesson
stops.campa: One of her hearers falls openly in love with her. Music, he is told, will not cure him, and she will not have philosophy mistaken for the body that carries it. Before the school she brings out the cloth of her own menstruation and casts it at his feet: this is what you love, young man, and it is nothing beautiful. The suitor is converted by shame to a better longing. Damascius sets the scene down without blinking; the canon keeps it as her fiercest theorem: that the soul is the only object worth desire.
suggested_refs: Damascius' Life of Isidore, the suitor episode (Suda)
sources: Damascius, Life of Isidore (Suda, s.v. Hypatia)

stops.name: Constantinople, the silver astrolabe
stops.campa: Synesius, in the capital three years pleading Cyrene's taxes before the emperor, courts the great with the only wealth he trusts: an instrument. He presents to Paeonius a planispheric astrolabe in silver, the heavens flattened onto a disc by the projection Hypatia taught him, her science travelling now in a courtier's baggage, the earliest such instrument the record knows. The gift is a sermon: astronomy, he writes, is itself a venerable science and a ladder toward the ineffable.
stops.quote: It is a work of my own devising, including all that she, my most revered teacher, helped to contribute.
stops.quote_source: Synesius, To Paeonius, on the Gift of an Astrolabe (De dono astrolabii)
suggested_refs: Synesius, 'Ad Paeonium de dono astrolabii'
earliest surviving planispheric astrolabes

stops.name: Cyrene, the hydroscope
stops.campa: Sick in his own country, with barbarians raiding the Pentapolis, Synesius writes to Alexandria for an instrument to weigh water. He describes it exactly, a cylindrical tube like a flute, notched in a perpendicular line, a cone fitted at the end, and asks his teacher to have it cast in brass. It is the first description of the hydrometer in the literature of the world, and it is a letter home: when the body fails, one writes to the Philosopher, who knows how all things are measured.
stops.quote: I am in such evil fortune that I need a hydroscope. See that one is cast in brass for me and put together.
suggested_refs: Synesius, Letter 15, first description of the hydrometer

stops.name: Cyrene, 'even there shall I remember thee'
stops.campa: The letters keep crossing the sea, each one addressed as to an oracle: to the Philosopher. Synesius, hemmed by war and losses, reaches for Homer to say what she is to him: the words Achilles keeps for Patroclus he gives to his teacher, a vow that memory of her will outlast the soul's forgetting. Alexandria, he writes elsewhere, is heaven to him because Hypatia is in it. The canon has no portrait of her face; it has this instead, which is more.
stops.quote: Even though there shall be utter forgetfulness of the dead in Hades, even there shall I remember thee, my dear Hypatia.
suggested_refs: Synesius, Letter 124
Iliad XXII.389-390, the vow echoed

stops.name: Alexandria, the episcopal throne: Cyril enthroned
stops.campa: Theophilus dies on the fifteenth of October and the city fights over his chair. Soldiers back the archdeacon Timothy; the crowd carries the day for the nephew, Cyril, who is enthroned on the third day amid tumult. Socrates notes the change at once: the bishopric of Alexandria goes beyond its sacerdotal bounds and takes on the flavor of secular rule. The Novatian churches are shut, their vessels seized. In the prefect's palace, Orestes begins to keep count.
suggested_refs: Socrates Scholasticus, Ecclesiastical History VII.7

stops.name: Ptolemais, the bishop's last letter: mother, sister, teacher
stops.campa: Synesius is bishop of Ptolemais now, and broken: his sons are dead, his city besieged, his body failing. From his bed he dictates a last letter across the water to the one court of appeal he has never doubted. He calls her everything a soul can be to a soul, mother, sister, teacher, benefactress, and asks after the friends of the lecture room as a dying man asks after paradise. He will not live to see the year 415. The canon counts this mercy.
stops.quote: I am dictating this letter to you from my bed, but may you receive it in good health, mother, sister, teacher, and withal benefactress, and whatsoever is honoured in name and deed.
suggested_refs: Synesius, Letter 16, the deathbed letter

stops.name: Alexandria, the Jewish quarter emptied
stops.campa: A quarrel over theatre dancers becomes a massacre in the night, and the answer to the massacre is an expulsion: Cyril leads the multitude against the synagogues, and the Jews of Alexandria, settled since Alexander marked the walls, are driven from the city, their goods pillaged. Orestes, who has lost a working city, writes his fury to the emperor; Cyril writes his own account. The two powers of Alexandria will not be reconciled, and every citizen must now know whose man he is. Hypatia's door stays open to both, which is already an accusation.
suggested_refs: Socrates Scholasticus VII.13, the expulsion of the Jews

stops.name: Alexandria, the street ambush of the prefect
stops.campa: Five hundred monks come down from Nitria into the city and stop the prefect's chariot in the street. They call Orestes pagan and idolater; he protests his baptism at Constantinople; the monk Ammonius opens his head with a stone. The crowd rescues the bleeding prefect, Ammonius dies under torture, and Cyril lays the body in a church and names him Thaumasius, the Wonderful: a martyr made of an assassin. Even the sober Christians, Socrates admits, will not accept it. The parabalani, the bishop's corps of bearers, learn the lesson: stones work.
suggested_refs: Socrates Scholasticus VII.14, Ammonius renamed Thaumasius

stops.name: Alexandria, the whisper: the woman who binds the prefect
stops.campa: The slander moves through the churches ahead of the knives: it is the woman who prevents the reconciliation of bishop and prefect; she has beguiled Orestes; she reads the stars; she is devoted, the hostile chronicle will say, to magic, astrolabes and instruments of music. Envy, says Damascius, armed itself against her. The astronomy that was a ladder to God in Synesius' letters becomes sorcery in the mouths of the parabalani. In Lent of this year the whisper will be given hands.
suggested_refs: John of Nikiu, Chronicle 84.87-103 (the hostile witness)

stops.name: Alexandria, the street: dragged from the chariot
stops.campa: It is Lent, the fourth year of Cyril's episcopate, the tenth consulship of Honorius. Hypatia is riding home through her city as she has for forty years, in the open, unguarded, because a philosopher fears nothing in the streets she has taught. A mob of the sworn men waylays the chariot, Peter the Reader at their head. Hands that carry the sick for the bishop pull the old woman down onto the stones. The city that doted on her looks away, and the chariot stands empty in the road.
suggested_refs: Socrates Scholasticus VII.15
the parabalani in the Codex Theodosianus XVI.2.42-43

stops.name: Alexandria, the Caesareum: the tiles and the oyster-shells
stops.campa: They drag her into the Caesareum, the temple Cleopatra raised to a deified Caesar and the bishops made a cathedral, the obelisks of Egypt still standing at its door. There they strip the Philosopher naked before the altar of the new god and murder her with ostraka, the sharp tiles and oyster-shells of the harbour city, flaying her while she still breathes. It is martyrdom, and the canon knows it: a witness killed in a sanctuary for the crime of wisdom. They tear the body limb from limb.
suggested_refs: Cleopatra's Needles, the obelisks of the Caesareum (now London and New York)
Socrates Scholasticus VII.15

stops.name: Alexandria, Cinaron: the burning
stops.campa: They carry the mangled limbs out to the place called Cinaron and burn them, as Theophilus' men burned the limbs of Serapis a generation before: the philosopher and the god given the same funeral by the same city. Nothing is left for a tomb; the fire is meant to end her as the axe was meant to end the temple. But smoke is a translation, not an erasure. What burns at Cinaron does not disperse: the canon is already carrying her elsewhere, and the city will learn under what name.
suggested_refs: Socrates Scholasticus VII.15, 'a place called Cinaron'

stops.name: Alexandria, the city after: the epitaph of the historians
stops.campa: The lecture hall stands empty through Eastertide. Socrates the historian, a churchman himself, sets down the verdict the Church cannot evade: this affair brought no small opprobrium upon Cyril and upon the whole Alexandrian church, for nothing can be farther from the spirit of Christianity than massacre. Damascius names Cyril outright. The philosophers begin to leave Alexandria; the imperial court trims the parabalani's numbers and forbids them the theatres and the council hall: a law standing where a woman stood. Alexandria does not recover the century of philosophy it loses with her.
suggested_refs: Codex Theodosianus XVI.2.42 (the parabalani restrained, 416)
Socrates Scholasticus VII.15
